slides.title: Study Overview
slides.text:
Background

• Barilla is a family-owned, 145-year-old international food company with an iconic brand and leading category share of pasta in the US.
• Barilla is looking to approach the Pasta aisle with fresh eyes and contemporized insights to support new hypotheses on assortment and merchandising strategies.
• Vista Grande has a suite of services, underpinned by its flagship Category Choice Architecture® framework, to cover the full spectrum of Barilla's needs while being a consultative thinking partner on how to activate the key insights and quantify their potential benefits.

Objectives / Approach

Vista Grande's Category Choice Architecture® framework was leveraged to gain insights into the following areas:
• How do shoppers desire the broad assortment of products? (Emphasis on key attributes, orientation, navigation, consideration sets)
• Who are today's pasta shoppers? (Emphasis on attitudinal dimensions)
• Why do they shop for pasta? (Emphasis on occasions for use and purchase drivers)
• Where do they shop to satisfy their need? (Emphasis on retailer, channel and reasons why)
• What tradeoffs are shoppers willing and unwilling to make? (Emphasis on substitution)

Additionally, the solution includes channel-specific Purchase Decision Hierarchies, Category Demand Structures, and a cloud-based Choice Analyzer dashboard.

slides.title: Objectives / Approach
slides.text:
• Category Choice Architecture® is applied with a broad lens covering all types of pasta products for leading Mass, Club, Grocery, Natural, Discount, and eCommerce retailers.
• Deliverables include channel-specific Purchase Decision Hierarchies, Decision Trees, and a Choice Analyzer dashboard, enabling hypothesis generation and compelling merchandising strategies.

slides.title: Research Design
slides.text:
The study was designed for coverage of key targets, channels, and categories:
• Channels: Mass, Club, Grocery, Natural, Discount, and eCommerce with Purchase Decision Hierarchies and Decision Trees for leading retailers/channels.
• Target: Past year purchasers of dry pasta and individuals with primary or shared grocery shopping responsibility.
• Sample: N = 4,013 respondents with representative demographics.
• Method: 15-minute web-based/mobile survey featuring a Category Choice Architecture® shopping simulation.
• Coverage: 77 retailers, 57 brands, and 557 products.

slides.title: Contextual Shopping Simulation
slides.text:
This slide describes a 15-minute primary research survey simulating the full customer journey. Steps include:
• Picking a retailer and stating why it was selected.
• Selecting attributes to form a consideration set.
• Adding products to the cart and checking out.
• Explaining purchase rationale including intended usage.
• Selecting substitutes if the original choice is unavailable.

slides.title: Retailer Coverage
slides.text: The simulation covers 77 retailers, ensuring a comprehensive view of the channels where consumers shop for dry pasta.

slides.title: Product / Brand Coverage
slides.text: A total of 557 products across 57 brands were evaluated, providing deep insights into the product and brand landscape in the pasta category.

slides.title: Purchase Motivations By Brand
slides.text: This slide shows the competitive landscape of brand purchase motivations. It details which brands are most trusted and chosen by consumers, highlighting factors such as high quality, texture, authenticity, and premium positioning. It also presents data on the percentage of respondents who substitute a product with the same brand.

slides.title: Product Specific Purchase Motivations by Domestic vs Imported
slides.text: This slide compares purchase motivations when choosing domestic versus imported pasta. Consumers select imported pasta for reasons like high quality, authentic taste, and premium attributes, while domestic options are chosen for their value proposition.

slides.title: Previously Purchased vs. First Time Purchasing
slides.text: Over half of consumers make a specific product choice at the shelf, indicating strong in-store activation potential. Most consumers have previously purchased the product, while a smaller segment are first-time buyers or unsure.

slides.title: Planned vs. Impulse Purchase of Product
slides.text: This slide examines the nature of the purchase decision. The majority of respondents plan their purchase—either with a specific product in mind or just a product type—while a small fraction make impulse or unplanned purchases.

slides.title: Summary of Purchase Motivations by Price/Quality Tier
slides.text: This slide summarizes key purchase motivations across different price/quality segments. Premium shoppers tend to value high quality, taste, and brand trust; mainstream shoppers focus on good value and preferred attributes; and value shoppers emphasize practical considerations like price and package size.

slides.title: Two Views of Shopper Decision Trees
slides.text: This slide presents two complementary views of shopper decision trees covering assortment strategies, competitive set identification, incrementality, SKU rationalization, and shopper marketing strategies. It highlights the two main components: NAVIGATION and SUBSTITUTION.

slides.title: Primary Lens for Shopping Dry Pasta
slides.text: The primary lens for shopping dry pasta is through Shape/Variety, followed by Pasta Type and then Price Tier (Value, Mainstream, Premium). Brand is the fourth attribute. Additional filters include Package Size, Package Type, Pasta Color/Flavor, and Domestic vs Imported.

slides.title: Decision Hierarchies Overview
slides.text: Decision hierarchies differ based on the product purchased. For Mainstream, Premium, and Imported products, Brand plays a more prominent role; for Value items, Price is dominant; and for Premium products, Pasta Type is prioritized. The chart below summarizes the hierarchy by Price Tier and Domestic vs Imported.

charts.chartTitle: Purchase Decision Hierarchies by Price Tier and Domestic/Imported

slides.title: Purchase Decision Hierarchies by Age
slides.text: This slide breaks down purchase decision hierarchies across age groups. All age groups use Pasta Shape/Variety as the primary filter, but younger shoppers (Gen Z and Younger Millennials) place greater emphasis on Price Tier, whereas older shoppers (Older Millennials, Gen X, Boomers) prioritize Pasta Type as the secondary filter. Additional filters such as Brand, Package Size, Package Type, and Domestic vs Imported are also considered.

slides.title: Top Attribute Considerations
slides.text: This slide details the top attribute considerations when shopping for dry pasta. Overall, 'Pasta Shape/Variety' is the highest considered attribute at 74%, followed by 'Routine/Regular (NET)' at 72%. Additional considerations include 'Oven/Baked (NET)' at 18% and 'Creative (NET)' at 16%. The slide then lists specific pasta types with their respective consideration percentages.

charts.chartTitle: Top Attribute Considerations for Dry Pasta

slides.title: While Brand is only a tertiary attribute overall, Barilla is the overwhelmingly most considered brand nationally
slides.text: This slide indicates that although shoppers primarily rely on factors such as Pasta Shape/Variety, Price Tier, and Pasta Type, when brand is considered it overwhelmingly favors Barilla on a national level. Detailed numeric data for this slide was not provided in the extract.

slides.title: Brand Consideration by Region
slides.text: When seeking out specific brands, Barilla is the clear leader, while secondary brand preferences vary by region. The chart below provides a regional breakdown of brand consideration percentages among respondents.

slides.title: Brand Loyalty and Substitution
slides.text: X1. Please select up to 3 products you might substitute if your original choice were unavailable. This slide presents two sets of data: the first shows the percentage of respondents who substituted with the same brand, and the second shows the percentage who substituted with a Barilla product when their first choice was unavailable. The data highlights that Barilla is a leader in both brand loyalty and substitution.

slides.title: Executive Summary
slides.text:
In a crowded dry pasta marketplace, Barilla stands alone as the clear category leader. However, there are opportunities for continued growth. Pasta is ubiquitous with high purchase frequency – over half of consumers eat store-bought pasta weekly or more often. Regular white pasta remains dominant, but many are open to alternatives like whole wheat and pasta with added protein, especially among Gen Z and Millennials.
IMPLICATION: Continue to stock traditional products and focus on younger consumers to establish Barilla as a leader in the Better For You space.

slides.title: Executive Summary (cont'd)
slides.text:
Dry pasta is purchased through many channels, with Grocery and Walmart as the dominant retailers. Online shopping is chosen by only about 1 in 10 consumers, emphasizing the importance of the in-store experience. IMPLICATION: Engage Grocery and Walmart with data reinforcing Barilla's in-store leadership, while also considering an online strategy. Additionally, most consumers make a specific product choice at the shelf, highlighting in-store activation opportunities.
IMPLICATION: Use pricing, promotion, packaging, and brand messaging to activate in-store shoppers.

slides.title: Sample Composition
slides.text: Large, diverse sample (N = 4,013) allows for comparisons across key demographics. The slide details age distribution, income, population density, and geographic region.

slides.title: Annual Purchase Frequency of Dry Pasta Types
slides.text: After regular white pasta, whole wheat, pasta with added protein, and oven cuts are bought most frequently on an annual basis. Pasta types like legume, gluten-free, and quick cook are bought less frequently, with less than half of respondents purchasing them in the past year.

slides.title: Important Factors When Buying Dry Pasta
slides.text: This slide presents the factors influencing the purchase of dry pasta. Consumers rank factors by importance when choosing their top three considerations. The data reveals that the best deal from a price/value perspective is the singular most important factor, followed by taste, household preference, cooking performance, and nutritional/quality attributes. Two charts are provided: one summarizing the top three factors overall and a detailed ranking table of factors across first, second, and third choices.
